transcript.text: You know when you went to the Shetland Islands last year, Paul? Did you go by ferry or did you fly?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: We went by ferry, Tammy. I prefer driving to flying – the journey feels like part of the holiday.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Mmm. Which ferry company did you use?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: There's only one – it's called Northern Ferries. The ferries all leave from Aberdeen.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: How frequent are they?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: The service is pretty limited – there's only one ferry leaving every evening in summer anyway, seven days a week – I'm not sure about the winter months. They may only run on four or five days then.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: OK. So it's an overnight trip. I quite like that idea. Leaving at night and waking up as you arrive on the island. Can you remember how much you paid for your tickets?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: They were really cheap and four people and a car worked out at just under £250.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Really? I was expecting it to be more like £400 during the peak season.
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: So was I. It's great value. It's a good idea to book in advance because I think they get booked up quite quickly – especially during the school holidays.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Yes, I suppose so. I'm just not 100% sure of our plans yet. What if I had to cancel?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: That could be a problem. I don't think it's their policy to give refunds – just a voucher – which you can use at a later date. But you have to cancel a month in advance to get that.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Right. Well we need to make up our minds quickly then.
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: You'd want to book a cabin too. We booked too late to get a cabin with a window. They're more expensive but much nicer than the inner cabins. You don't have to book a cabin at all but I think it's worth paying for. They also have luxury cabins, which are only for two people and have a TV – but I wouldn't bother with those.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: No, I agree.
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: The only other thing I can think of is to make sure you bring snacks for the kids. The selection on board is quite limited and not that healthy either.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Mmm. What about wifi on board? Is that any good?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: Not really. So it's best to bring some books for them.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: OK. We may need to bring the dog if I can't get anyone to look after him.
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: We brought ours and it was fine. The kennels on board are OK – they're quite big – you just need to provide a blanket.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Uhuh. Sounds good.
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: It was all very easy really – and it was quite an adventure for the kids. They loved being on the sea at night and in the morning keeping a lookout for dolphins – we saw loads.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Oh, the kids would love that!
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: One other thing. We arrived in Aberdeen hours before the ferry was due to leave so we decided to go somewhere else rather than hang around at the port for so long.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Where did you go?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: Drum Castle.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: I've never heard of it. Is that spelt like the instrument?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: Yeah. It's really worth visiting. It's got an impressive tower and beautiful gardens and ancient woodland.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Sounds lovely. Does it have a restaurant?
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: It's only got a coffee shop – no restaurant. We looked up restaurants in the area and found an Italian one in a village nearby. I can check the name of it for you if you're interested.
transcript.speaker: PAUL

transcript.text: Oh thanks Paul that would be ....
transcript.speaker: TAMMY

transcript.text: Good evening everyone.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: My name's Jon and I run Veg Out, a street food business selling vegan food.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Since 2012 I've been travelling all around the country cooking vegan food in my converted van and selling it at all kinds of outdoor events.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: I'm here to give you some advice based on my experience.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: The good news is that there's never been a better time to start your own street food business.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Street food continues to grow in popularity.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: I think there are a couple of reasons for this.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: The first is that street food is a reaction against fast food.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Street food ranges from high quality burgers to vegan curries and everything in between.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: But while fast food is cheap and easy to find, it's not particularly good for you.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: It's also the same everywhere.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: What you get with street food on the other hand is something different.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: People like the idea of trying something they can't get anywhere else.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: They also like seeing food prepared in front of them and which hasn't come straight out of a freezer.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: You need to think about the best place to sell your street food.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: People always think music festivals are an obvious place to start but the cost of renting a space can be huge.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: And there's always a lot of competition.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Food markets, on the other hand, are great because customers are always really interested in food and give great feedback.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: And if you can get a spot in your local park – fantastic.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Usually very relaxed but with lots of customers passing by.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Once you get established you'll start getting asked to do parties – which can be really challenging but lots of fun.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Having street food at weddings has become quite fashionable too – but you need to really know what you're doing as everything needs to be perfect.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Setting up a street food business costs a lot less than opening a restaurant or café but you'll have to buy some basic equipment.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: I'd try to get things like hobs and fridges second hand if you can.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: You can replace them with better quality stuff if your business takes off.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Renting is another option but you'll end up spending more money rather than saving it.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: You've probably got a good idea about the food you're planning to sell.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: I expect you've done some research to find out if anyone else is selling a similar product.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: And you'll have thought about any possible allergies to nuts or eggs etc.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: But there's one thing people don't always think about and that's how you're going to serve it.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: On a plate?
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: In a bag?
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Will you provide a fork?
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Will it all be easily recyclable or reusable?
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: It's got to be easy to eat and look attractive or customers won't come back.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Once you get started, you should be prepared for things to go wrong.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Every business faces problems and here are a few examples from street food businesses that I know.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: My friends who run Thai Basil started by juggling their street food business with their day jobs in a restaurant.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Their work-life balance was non-existent as they were working til midnight in the restaurant all week and then took their food truck to markets on their days off.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: The owners of Basque found it was hard to make a profit because the price of fish – essential for some of their dishes – was so high.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: And it was hard to charge customers a lot more for those dishes.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: So they had to stop focussing on fish dishes and include more vegetarian food.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: The owners of Lou's kitchen were making salads to order from their van and some of their dishes were quite complicated.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: At one of their first events they ended up with people standing in a long queue for more than 15 minutes – and many of them lost patience.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: So make sure whatever you offer can be served quickly and efficiently.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: The owners of Chip Chop had found a perfect venue near a beach where there weren't any other street food trucks.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: But what they hadn't realised was that they'd need a special licence – which individual businesses don't need at markets or festivals.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: It was a complicated process and in the end they gave up.
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: So I hope that's given you a flavour of ....
transcript.speaker: JON

transcript.text: Shall we go through our research for our sustainable fashion project?
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Good idea. I think I've done enough reading now.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Me too. I've learnt such a lot about what sustainability actually means.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Mmm, same for me with ethical fashion. I didn't really appreciate the difference between that and sustainable fashion before doing this research.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: I know – most people use these terms interchangeably – but in fact the difference is quite distinct when you think about it. Sustainable relates to the environment and ethical relates more to the way workers or animals are treated.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: I totally understand why people get confused, though. There are so many other terms used – like 'eco- friendly', which is actually quite meaningless.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: And the way companies use these terms when describing their products doesn't help. They're often deliberately vague, I think, and don't provide enough information about how their products are made.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: It was interesting to read about the debates surrounding wool production and how ethical and sustainable that is. It's generally considered to be sustainable because it's a natural product.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: And it also lasts a long time and can be recycled. All very positive. But I wasn't convinced by the argument that wool production is sustainable because it doesn't use many chemicals – what about all the fungicides and insecticides used in sheep farming?
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Good point. And I couldn't find any evidence for the claim about sheep farming being better for the environment than cattle farming.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: No – they're both really bad. I read different reports about how unethical it is to even shear sheep. Some people say it's cruel but as long as the sheep are kept in good condition I can't see anything wrong with it.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Me neither.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Shall we talk about some of the semi-synthetic new fabrics now?
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: OK, let's do that.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Let's start with Lyocell, I've been reading about that.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Yeah, that's the one produced from the pulp of eucalyptus trees, isn't it?
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Yes, and what happens with that is really impressive. Over 99% of dissolving agents used in the manufacturing process are used again.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Yeah. Now, there are a few semi-synthetic fabrics that I'd never heard of. Like Cupro, for example.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Made from byproducts of the cotton industry to create a kind of vegan silk. But I'm not sure how sustainable this really is as there are so many reports of pollution caused by the manufacturing process.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Mmm. It doesn't compare favourably with all the other sustainable fabrics we've looked at, no.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Bamboo is one fabric we're all familiar with. But I didn't know that it was only organic bamboo that's truly sustainable.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Me neither. Apparently, the manufacturing process for a significant proportion of bamboo is chemically quite intensive – which obviously can be quite damaging.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: EcoVero is an example of a semi-synthetic fabric which is becoming really popular.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Probably because manufacturing causes 50 percent fewer emissions and takes up half as much energy as conventional fabrics. That saves production costs as well as being better for the environment.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: That's true. I think demand for cork will continue to grow. It works really well in vegan shoes and bags.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Mmm and it's the only fabric that's fundamentally sustainable – the cork trees it comes from are renewable and the product itself is both recyclable and biodegradable – which is unique.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: And the harvesting process is actually good for the trees. There are no downsides to using this source at all.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Hemp is another really good sustainable fabric from a natural source.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: Yes. Did you know that clothes made from hemp protect the wearer from the sun and it's also antibacterial?
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: No, I didn't. But I did read that it's quite hard to grow, so perhaps that's why it's not as common as you'd think.
transcript.speaker: MADDY

transcript.text: I'm sure that'll change.
transcript.speaker: RYAN

transcript.text: Today I'm going to talk about invasive species.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Let me start by saying what an invasive species is and what it's not.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Invasive species are any animal or plant that is introduced into an environment by humans, and which is then harmful to that environment.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It's important to be clear that not all introduced species are invasive.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Many introduced – or non-native – species thrive in new areas without posing any threat.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In some cases, invasive species have changed the natural world beyond recognition, so let's look at the different ways they can be problematic.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: First of all, invasive species may eat native species, or sometimes they may bring a disease with them, which native species have never faced before and therefore have no defences against.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Often the invasive species breed very quickly – which further adds to the problem of native species losing their sources of food.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Species invasions are one of the biggest causes of damage in an ecosystem, actually putting its survival at risk.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So, how do invasive species spread?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Without a doubt, the biggest cause is human activity.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This could be intentional, or it could be accidental, such as when people who've been on holiday in another country come back with, say, the seeds of plants on their clothes or shoes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Plants and animals, especially insects, arrive in or on the cargo of ships, and then escape into their new 'home'.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But sometimes humans deliberately move animals and plants around the world, for example to use them to control pests on farms, or to be pets.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This can go very wrong if those animals and plants move into wild settings and start breeding or begin growing in ways that weren't predicted.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Let's now look at an example of an invasive species here in Australia: Rhinella marina is a species of toad that was deliberately introduced from Hawaii in 1935 as a form of biological control.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It was hoped that the toads would eat the grey-backed beetles responsible for destroying crops of sugar on many of the plantations.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: At first, just a handful of toads were released by scientists into Queensland, but this number soon grew as other states followed suit.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Within two years, 62,000 young toads had been released into the wild.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The toads did nothing to protect the plantations, but they did reproduce rapidly and could soon be found all over the northern half of the country.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The toads are poisonous at every stage of their life cycle, and anything that eats them will die.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: My second example regarding invasive species is the United Kingdom.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Actually, there are more than three- thousand invasive species there, including some that are extremely common.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some invasive plants, such as Japanese knotweed, have had a devastating impact on parts of the UK.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Gardeners in the nineteenth century considered it a beautiful ornamental plant – which it is, when it's kept under control – but it soon spread into the countryside and remains a problem even to this day as it's so hard to eradicate.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another invasive plant is rhododendrons, which can be found in UK parks and woodlands.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Their introduction dates back to 1763, but they're now seen as harmful because they block out so much light that native wild flowers can't grow beneath them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And then there are grey squirrels, which are one invasive species almost everyone in the UK will have come across.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They were brought to the UK from North America and introduced to private estates around the 1870s but are now found everywhere, from forests to city squares.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Grey squirrels have outcompeted the smaller, native red squirrels.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They both eat the same food, and the grey squirrels carry a type of virus that is deadly to the red squirrels.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Red squirrel populations have collapsed, and there are only a handful of sites left in the UK where they're found.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: An important question for ecologists worldwide is, what can we do to tackle the problem of invasive species?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The first step in controlling invasive species is learning about the behaviour of new species coming into the country.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Monitoring is an important part of this, so that we can know if the new species begins to have a negative impact in its new environment.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One effective way to keep track of invasive species is to create a database for the whole country.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: That way, all relevant authorities and agencies can share important information and take whatever action's needed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But the public also have a vital role to play in this process.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: They should be encouraged to photograph harmful species – because this helps with identification – and then to report when and where these were observed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But it's important to tell people not to destroy or even touch what they've found.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Now, I'm going to move on to ...
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
